tagline.text: A free city park in downtown Davao with a durian dome and a national museum

location.label: Location
location.text: J. Palma Gil Street, Poblacion District, Davao City

children.text: People's Park is a roughly 4-hectare cultural park in downtown Davao, close to City Hall. Entry is free, and the Durian Dome, sculptures by Kublai Millan, a giant Philippine Eagle sculpture and the National Museum of the Philippines–Davao, which opened in 2024, all sit in one compound.

People's Park Davao is an urban park of about 4 hectares (roughly 9.9 acres) in the Poblacion District at the heart of Davao City. It began as the PTA Grounds (the Palaruang Panlungsod, or city playground), a venue for sports and events. Conversion work started in July 2006, and the park was formally inaugurated on December 15, 2007. Wikipedia puts the cost at about ₱71 million, while other travel guides say more than ₱72 million. The name was picked from 918 entries in a city government naming contest.

The first thing you see at the entrance is the dome shaped like a durian. The durian is Davao's best-known fruit and something of a city emblem, and the dome serves as a visitor center and exhibit space. Further in you will find a brick promenade, ponds, an artificial waterfall, a small bridge, a children's playground and a fountain lit up at night, with large sculptures of Indigenous figures by Mindanao sculptor Kublai Millan scattered throughout. The best known is a large replica of the Philippine Eagle, big enough for several people to sit beneath it.

On December 1, 2024, the National Museum of the Philippines–Davao (NMP-Davao) opened inside the park, in a six-storey building modeled on the durian. Its displays cover natural history, geology, and the life rituals and textiles of Mindanao's Indigenous peoples, which lifted what was once simply a walking park into a starting point for exploring Davao's culture. Museum entry is also free, so you can fill half a day at no cost.

After dark, the Roxas Night Market sets up on the road beside the park, with grilled food, snacks and secondhand clothing stalls. The park itself is less a flashy tourist attraction than a living space where locals stroll and rest. It suits a short afternoon stop of one or two places on a Davao city itinerary. Hours and rules mentioned here can change, so check the latest announcements before you go.

This durian-shaped building near the park entrance works as a visitor center. According to Wikipedia it covers about 425 square meters and holds a bamboo garden inside, and there is also a gallery of photos of Davao's tribes and events such as the Kadayawan Festival. It is the classic backdrop for photos of the park.

The park's most famous sculpture stands near the path leading to the children's playground. The Philippine Eagle is a symbol of Davao, so many visitors pose for photos in front of it. You can see real eagles at the
Philippine Eagle Center

Most of the park's large sculptures are the work of Davao sculptor Kublai Millan. Many show figures that evoke Indigenous communities, alongside colorful, fantastical forms. They are the artist's interpretation, so it is best not to take them as a complete picture of Davao's many tribes.

This six-storey durian-shaped building opened on December 1, 2024. Reported displays include Victorio Edades's large painting "Davao Industries" on the ground floor, geology, biodiversity and a mounted Philippine Eagle on the second, Mindanao Indigenous life rituals on the third, and textile traditions on the fourth. The fifth floor is run by Museo Dabawenyo, the city's own museum.

A brick promenade runs where the old athletics oval used to be, good for jogging or an easy walk. Wikipedia describes the dancing fountain here as the first in Mindanao. It is not guaranteed to run every night, so treat it as a bonus if you catch it.

The ponds, a small artificial waterfall and a bridge make for pleasant shady rest spots. The playground has swings, slides and monkey bars, and many families bring their children here. The park also has a children's library, a learning center and a sunken garden.

When the park opened, 1,101 species of plants and trees were reported along its five avenues. Highlights include tropical plantings and walls lit up in the shape of waling-waling orchids. In the heat of the day, it is easiest to walk in the shade of the trees.

This night market near the park is reported to run daily from 6 PM to midnight. Vendors sell charcoal-grilled food, local snacks, secondhand clothes and accessories, and there are massage shops too. Carry your bag in front against pickpockets and bring small change.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The museum and a park stroll

children.text: Start with the National Museum Davao. Go in the morning while the museum is open, and check the latest notice for its opening days before you go. Begin with the large painting and the hanging gongs installation on the ground floor, then work up through the floors for about
1–1.5 hours
Photograph the Durian Dome and the sculptures around the entrance. The park is said to open at 1 PM, so it works best to see the museum first in the morning.
Once the park opens, pass the bag check at the entrance and go in. Walk around the ponds, the waterfall and the Philippine Eagle sculpture.
Take a lap along the brick promenade, look in at the children's library and the sunken garden, then rest on a shaded bench.
The indoor museum suits the heat of midday and the open-air park suits the late afternoon. The museum and the park keep different hours, so a check the day before saves a wasted trip.

items.title: Evening route
items.subtitle: The park and the night market

children.text: Enter the park as the sun gets low and walk the promenade. It is less hot than during the day, and the lights come on one by one.
Head to the Roxas Night Market next to the park for grilled food and snacks. Bring cash in small bills.
Walk to nearby San Pedro Cathedral, or take a ride-hailing taxi back to your hotel.
The night market area gets crowded after dark, so keep your belongings in front of you and avoid empty side streets late at night.

items.title: Downtown Davao full day
items.subtitle: From the cathedral to the park and the market

children.text: Visit
San Pedro Cathedral, Davao
first. It is a place of worship, so dress modestly.
Walk over to the National Museum Davao and see the exhibits.
After lunch, stroll the park and see the Durian Dome and the eagle sculpture.
Finish with dinner at the Roxas Night Market.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO). Airlines and schedules change with the season, so check when you book.
From the airport to the city, take a taxi or a ride-hailing taxi; fares and travel time vary with traffic. A 2011 guide quoted a taxi at about
and a jeepney at
, but prices have probably risen since.
The park is in the middle of the city, so if you stay at a downtown hotel you can often walk there.
A taxi or ride-hailing taxi is the easiest option. Give the destination as "People's Park, J. Palma Gil Street."
Jeepneys also pass through this area, so tell the driver you want to get off near Palma Gil Street.
From downtown hotels you can walk in good weather, but be ready for midday heat and sudden rain.
Parking is reported to be limited, so a taxi is easier than bringing a car.

The park is mostly an outdoor stroll, so the drier season is the most comfortable. Davao is known as a part of the Philippines relatively less affected by typhoons, but showers can come any time of year, so bring an umbrella.

The biggest event season is the Kadayawan Festival in August. The park is known as a venue for the Dula Kadayawan tribal games during the festival, so it pairs well if your dates line up. Crowds build during the festival, so book lodging and transport early.

Hotels in the Poblacion District within walking distance of the park are the most convenient. City Hall, San Pedro Cathedral and the markets are all clustered here, which suits an itinerary with a lot of walking. Prices vary widely, so check current rates and reviews on a booking site.

The signature food is the grilled food and snacks at the Roxas Night Market. Davao is famous for tropical fruit such as durian and pomelo, so if it is in season, try some at a fruit stall. Durian smells strong and is banned in many hotels and on public transport, so decide in advance where you will eat it.
Park rangers check bags at the entrance, so do not bring sharp objects such as knives.
An official listing gives park hours as 1 PM to 10 PM. Planning the morning around the museum fits the timing well.
Sources disagree on whether the National Museum closes on Mondays or opens daily. Check the museum's official notice or social media before you set out.
One valid ID per group is said to be required for museum entry, so carry your passport copy or another ID.
The park is a no-smoking zone, and violators may be penalized.
You may bring your own food, but it is important to take your trash with you or use the bins.
Some stretches have little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Carry small cash at the night market and wear your bag in front.
About
1–2 hours
is usually enough, and allow about
3 hours
if you also see the museum.
Opening hours, the museum's opening days and entry rules can change, so check the latest announcements before you visit.
There is a security check at the park entrance, so leave unnecessary items at your hotel.
The area around the night market is crowded late at night, so watch for pickpockets.
Reports say the museum closed briefly after the October 2025 earthquake and reopened on January 11, 2026. It can close for events or maintenance, so confirm before you go.
Outdoor activity is hard in the heat of the day, so use the morning or late afternoon.
Durian is banned in many hotels and indoor spaces because of its smell.
Davao's main cathedral is close to the park, in the same Poblacion District, and easy to visit on the same outing. It is a place of worship, so dress modestly.
A guide to Davao City as a whole, where you can combine downtown sights, markets and restaurants.
If you liked the park's eagle sculpture, this is where you go to see real eagles. It is best to plan it as a separate day trip from the city.
A good fit if you want to leave the city for a mountain park, but you will need separate transport.
